You make the share one hundred and nine parts and multiply the thirteen by one hundred and nine, then add eighty parts to that, which results in one thousand four hundred and ninety-seven, and the husband's portion is three hundred and twenty-seven.

If a woman leaves two sisters and a husband, and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's portion minus one-eighth of what remains of the estate after the legacy, the calculation for this is to establish the legal shares <note>original: al-faridah</note> out of twelve shares. Each sister receives one-third of what remains of the estate after the legacy. This is the estate minus the legacy. You know that one-eighth of what remains plus the legacy equals a sister's portion. One-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy. Therefore, one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy plus the legacy equals a sister's portion. That is one-eighth of the estate and seven-eighths of the legacy. The entire estate equals three-eighths of the estate plus three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. Subtract three-eighths from the estate, and five-eighths of the estate remains, equaling three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. The entire estate then equals five legacies and four-fifths of a legacy. Thus, the estate is twenty-nine, the legacy is five, and the portion is eight.

In another type of legacy: a man dies and leaves four sons, and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of one of his sons' portions, and to another man one-quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the legacy is taken only from the third.

In short, error regarding the Law is of two types: 

First, an error for which the person who is a practitioner of <term>nazar</term> <gloss>speculative investigation</gloss> is excused in the matter where the error occurred, just as a skilled physician is excused if he errs in the art of medicine, and a skilled judge is excused if he errs in judgment; but the one who is not a practitioner of that field is not excused. 

Second, an error for which no human being is excused. Before his time, the city belonged to Ashqiya Musa, but he surrendered it to King al-Nasir in exchange for compensation. Al-Nasir sent a commander and an army there, but later Sultan Badr al-Din took control of it, built his royal residence there, and his rule became firmly established.

I met this Sultan outside the city while he was returning from a hunt. I dismounted from my animal for him, so he dismounted from his animal and greeted me. He welcomed me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that if a traveler dismounts for them, they are pleased by his action and increase their honor toward him. However, if a traveler greets them while remaining mounted, they find it offensive and displeasing, and it becomes a reason for the traveler to be denied favor. This actually happened to me with one of them, and I regretted it later. When I had greeted him and remounted, he asked about my condition and my arrival. I entered the city with him, and he ordered the finest lodging to be prepared for me. He used to send abundant food, fruit, and sweets in silver trays <note>original: "tayāfīr"</note>, as well as candles, clothing, and horses, and he treated me with great excellence.

Our stay with him was not long, and we departed for the city of Aksaray <note>original: "Aqsara", spelled with a short "a" on the "alif", a silent "q", and a short "a" on both the "s" and "r"</note>. It is among the most beautiful and well-constructed cities in the land of the <term>Rum</term> <gloss>Anatolia/the Romans</gloss>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and orchards on every side. Three rivers cut through the city, and water flows through the houses. Inside the city are trees, grapevines, and many gardens. The famous rugs named after this city are manufactured there from sheep’s wool; there are none like them in any other country. From there, they are exported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks.

This city is under the authority of the King of Iraq <note>the Mongol Ilkhanate ruler</note>. I stayed there in the <term>zawiya</term> <gloss>lodge</gloss> of Sharif Husayn, the deputy there for Emir Arta. Arta is the deputy for the King of Iraq over the parts of the land of the <term>Rum</term> that he has conquered. This Sharif is one of the <term>Fityan</term> <gloss>members of the youth guilds</gloss> and has a large following. He showed us complete hospitality and acted with the same generosity as those before him.

Then we traveled to the city of Nigde <note>original: "Nakda", spelled with a short "a" on the "n", a silent "k", and a short "a" on the "d"</note>. It is one of the cities belonging to the King of Iraq. It is a heavily populated city, though some of it has fallen into ruin. It is divided by the river known as the Black River. It is a large river with three bridges over it: one inside the city and two outside. There are waterwheels both inside and outside the city to irrigate the orchards. Fruits there are abundant. # The reason we established the distance

from the meridian <note>original: "nisf al-nahar"</note> is because the <term>adjustment</term> <gloss>equation or correction</gloss> for the birth <note>referring to the calculation of the new moon or Molad</note> is easier through it than by working with horizons. The hours of the longest day for the latitude of Jerusalem <note>original: "Bayt al-Maqdis"</note> are fourteen hours and a fraction. The Jewish method using <term>seasonal hours</term> <gloss>unequal hours that vary based on the length of day and night</gloss> is not accurate unless the <term>conjunction</term> <gloss>the Molad or astronomical alignment of sun and moon</gloss> for the beginning of <term>Tishrei</term> <gloss>the first month of the Jewish civil year</gloss> occurs exactly at the autumnal equinox. This never happens exactly; rather, it precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we have demonstrated previously.

When we extract the time of the conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table which we analyzed according to their opinion, we proceed from that to the knowledge of the first day of the year and the determination of its quality—whether it is "defective," "regular," or "complete" <note>referring to the three possible lengths of the Jewish year: chasirah, kesidran, or shelemah</note>. We would have already determined whether the year is <term>ordinary</term> <gloss>a 12-month year</gloss> or <term>leap</term> <gloss>a 13-month intercalary year</gloss>.

We then search the Table of Limits <note>original: "Jadwal al-Hudud"</note> for a duration of the days of the week whose two boundaries encompass the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look in the column for leap years if it is a leap year, or the column for ordinary years if it is ordinary. When we find it, we find next to it the day of the week on which the year begins and its specific quality. Once we know the start of the year and its quality, and combine that quality with its status as ordinary or leap, we can determine the arrival of the first day of the following year.

If one asks how this mundane Great Bliss is the primary object of meditation, it is said: "That which is called Innate Joy," and so forth. If one then asks: "Since you are the primary Great Bliss to be accomplished, and the innate bliss of cyclic existence is not the object of accomplishment, why are you the primary object of accomplishment?" It is answered: "In that case, I..." and so forth.

The word "also" functions here to indicate the cause, because it establishes the primary truth in that very way. One accomplishes realization through an analogous example; therefore, the primary is designated as "I" in that context.

The "Consort" refers to the <term>Vajra Consort</term> <gloss>wisdom partner</gloss> and the "example consort." Consequently, the intentional meaning is that those who seek the bliss to be accomplished must definitely meditate on the <term>Devata-yoga</term> <gloss>Deity Yoga</gloss>. In this way...

The syllable <term>Ba</term> refers to the melting of the moon <note>original: "zla ba zhu ba", referring to the melting of bodhicitta or vital essence within the central channel</note>. All of this is explained in detail in the eighth chapter. As for what has not been explained previously: "What is meant by the term <term>Samvara</term> <gloss>Vow or Union</gloss>?" This is the remaining question. This serves as the inquiry. "Please explain," is the request being made. Regarding the reply, "What did he say?" 

The response begins with the phrase "The one called the Yogini." "The center of the body" refers to the navel. <term>A</term> is the first of the vowels. "Abiding" means abiding there eternally. "The Yogini" refers to <term>Nairatmya</term> <gloss>Lady of Selflessness</gloss>, and this is connected to the term <term>Samvara</term>. 

The meaning of the word <term>Samvara</term> <gloss>Union/Vow</gloss> is then explained. Regarding the phrase "Just as..." and so forth: just as it is on the outside, so too should it be viewed on the inside. The meaning is that the internal is not inferior to the external. Because the body is perfectly bound <note>original: "bsdams pa"</note> and because the supreme is perfectly gathered <note>original: "bsdus pa"</note>, the term <term>Samvara</term> <gloss>Union</gloss> is intended. Thus, it is shown here that just as there is the body of <term>Nairatmya</term>, so too the syllable <term>A</term> abides at the navel. 

"Vajra Bliss" refers to the <term>A</term> at the navel moving to the tip of the <term>Vajra</term> <gloss>the secret organ</gloss>. Furthermore, by the process of the syllable <term>Hum</term> moving from the heart down to the top of the <term>A</term>, that <term>Hum</term> is the Vajra Bliss. That is the <term>Mahamudra</term> <gloss>Great Seal</gloss>. This means the condensed forms of the Yogini and the Heruka. This itself is the Vajra Sense-source, which is the <term>Bodhicitta</term> <gloss>Enlightened Mind/Seminal Essence</gloss>. This itself is the Method. "Secret" refers to the meditative union of both the <term>A</term> and the <term>Hum</term>. 

The "external manifestation of the two" refers to the bodies of <term>Nairatmya</term> and <term>Heruka</term>, which is Great Joy. The phrase "Clearly demonstrating" means to establish and then show. 

Regarding the phrase "The Three Bodies" <note>original: "sku gsum", Trikaya</note>, these are the infinite Emanation Bodies <note>Nirmanakaya</note>, the infinite Truth Bodies <note>Dharmakaya</note>, and the infinite Enjoyment Bodies <note>Sambhogakaya</note> of the Buddhas. These three bodies are explained and demonstrated as being within the body. 

If one asks how that <term>Samvara</term> <gloss>Union</gloss> exists, it is in the form of <term>Chakras</term> <gloss>Energy Centers</gloss>. Specifically, it takes the form of the three wheels—Emanation and the others—in the configuration of sixty-four petals <note>at the navel</note>, eight petals <note>at the heart</note>, and sixteen petals <note>at the throat</note>. The complete realization of these three bodies is the Wisdom of Equality...

The "joy of emission" <note>the joy of creative emission or expansion</note> that occurs before the culmination of analytical investigation is "great passion." "Subsequently" means after that, or from that point on. "Great attachment" is the subsequent passion; it means the supreme joy at the culmination of analytical investigation. From this point onward, the sequences are mostly different. <meta>continues from previous page</meta> or, because they bind, they are called the <term>fetters</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: saṃyojana</gloss> that tie one to existence.

Regarding the phrase, "the mind is perfectly and completely liberated through right knowledge," the term "knowledge" refers to thorough understanding and realization. Thus, it is said that the mind is perfectly liberated through authentic realization.

Alternatively, "complete liberation" here refers to <term>faith</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: adhimukti</gloss>. The twentieth, likewise, perform the benefit of sentient beings and dwell by moving from Buddha-field to Buddha-field.

Furthermore, it is taught in two ways: the <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>nature of reality</gloss> of viewing things exactly as they truly are, and the <term>dharmata</term> of accomplishment.

The term "faultless" <note>original: "skyon med pa"</note> means "non-existent" in this context. When the entity of a fault does not exist, it is called "faultless."

Regarding the statement, "in inner emptiness, one does not truly perceive outer emptiness," this means that inner emptiness is empty by its own essential nature. It is not made empty by other forms of emptiness, such as outer emptiness. Therefore, one does not seek outer emptiness in order to make inner emptiness empty.

Likewise, one does not seek inner emptiness within outer emptiness to make it empty, because it is empty by its own essential nature. 

When training in this way, one should understand form, yet one should not become conceited about it. This means that since all phenomena are empty by their own nature, one should understand them as being merely names. Having understood them as merely names, one should not harbor conceit regarding these phenomena.

After teaching in this manner up to the unique qualities of a Buddha, it is then taught that a <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>hero of awakening</gloss> should not be conceited even about the <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>mind of awakening</gloss>. This explains the mind of awakening together with its qualities.

Regarding the phrase, "this mind is no-mind," the word "mind" refers to the <term>parikalpita</term> <gloss>conceptually constructed</gloss> mind. The perfected, unsurpassed, and perfectly complete mind of awakening, which has become the <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss>, is called "no-mind" because it transcends all characteristics of conceptualization and imagination, and thus lacks the characteristics of the ordinary mind.

Therefore, it is said that "the nature of the mind is clear light." The nature of the mind of the <term>dharmakaya</term> is clear light. Thus, the statement "it is no-mind" means it is not the conceptually constructed mind.

The phrase "it is neither possessed of passion nor free from passion" demonstrates that very nature of clear light. Previously, in the state of an ordinary being, passion and hatred <unclear>...</unclear>

In the state of purity, just as we speak of the sky being clear, this <term>sunyata</term> <gloss>emptiness</gloss> is also expressed. In the state of impurity, because it is not distinct from the ordinary <term>prithagjana</term> <gloss>immature being or worldling</gloss>, it is spoken of in terms such as form. However, in the state of purity, it is called emptiness. Therefore, the meaning is that there are no phenomena such as form that exist as something separate from emptiness. Thus, because there is no distinction between phenomena and their true nature <note>original: "dharmata"</note>, when the true nature is expressed through phenomena, form itself is called emptiness. When phenomena are used to express the true nature, emptiness is also called form. 

Alternatively, regarding the statement "form itself is emptiness and emptiness itself is form," emptiness refers to <term>tathata</term> <gloss>suchness</gloss>, which applies to the form of the true nature. Since those forms that are conceptually constructed <note>original: "parikalpita"</note> and mentally imagined <note>original: "vikalpita"</note> are utterly non-existent, and because it is improper to abide even in the perfected form <note>original: "parinispanna"</note>, it is said that "one should not abide in form." The same should be applied to feelings and the other aggregates.

The phrase "one should not abide in letters" means one should not abide in the syllables of the alphabet such as the letter **A**. The phrase "one should not abide in the actualization of letters" refers to the following: through relying on the syllables of the alphabet such as **A**, a <term>dharani</term> <gloss>incantatory or mnemonic</gloss> cognition arises which follows the meaning of non-arising. This is called the "actualization of letters," and the text teaches that one should not abide even in that. Because that <term>dharani</term> cognition is also originally unarisen, the letter **A** is described as the "gate to all phenomena," and it is through this description that actualization occurs.

As for this verbal expression, if certain Bodhisattvas with the sharpest faculties rely on this single meaning of non-arising and enter into it, it becomes the condition for their manifest and perfect awakening. Those with middling faculties rely on two letters and, by training in two verbal expressions, they proceed.

It is said that one generates <note>original: པ་བསྐྱེད་#དོ་</note> such motivation. After that, one begins the application that is consistent with donning the armor <note>refers to the armor of diligence or <term>saṃnāha-vīrya</term></note>; of this, it is said that one exerts oneself. Following that, even when great difficulties arise, one does not become discouraged but instead increases diligence itself; of this, it is said that one applies diligence. After that, having completely abandoned accomplishment through incorrect means, one abides in the authentic method; this is shown by these two phrases: "holds the mind firmly" and "perfectly places the mind."

In that regard, if the mind becomes sunken <note>referring to mental lethargy or <term>laya</term></note>, one holds it firmly by mentalizing the act of holding; thus, because it holds, it is called holding the mind firmly. If the mind becomes agitated <note>referring to mental excitement or <term>auddhatya</term></note>, one perfectly places it by mentalizing the act of withdrawing; this is called perfectly and thoroughly placing the mind.

Regarding the third section, the four bases of miraculous power <note>original: རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱི་རྐང་པ་བཞི་, Sanskrit: <term>ṛddhipāda</term></note> are called the bases of miraculous power because they serve as the foundation and support for the supramundane qualities known as miracle. These four are aspiration, diligence, intention, and discernment. In this way, when some individuals develop a great desire for the cultivation of virtuous qualities, they engage solely through the power of aspiration. Because there is no other mentalizing or thinking of certainties, the mind becomes one-pointed. The meditative concentration <note>original: ཏིང་#འཛིན་, Sanskrit: <term>samādhi</term></note> arising from the power of that aspiration is called the meditative concentration of aspiration.

When some individuals apply themselves through the diligence of the four authentic abandonments <note>Sanskrit: <term>samyakprahāṇa</term></note>, they apply themselves with the diligence that places them in virtue. As they engage in abandoning non-virtue and producing virtue, the mind becomes one-pointed. The meditative concentration arising from the power of that diligence is called the meditative concentration of diligence. When some individuals engage in training the mind, they perfectly place the mind through the causes of calm abiding <note>Sanskrit: <term>śamatha</term></note>, firm holding, and equanimity. Through the power of training the mind, the mind comes to rest in one-pointedness. The meditative concentration arising from the power of that intention <insert>is called the meditative concentration of intention.</insert>

The times of eating, the clothing, and all various enjoyments; and however many eons of burning occur in those world systems; and however many destructions by water, fire, and wind occur; the extent of the realm of space, and however many forms of stars exist; however many mountains, mountain clefts, rivers, lakes, and oceans exist; however many villages, cities, towns, districts, countries, and royal palaces exist; however many classifications of marketplaces exist; however many fields, parks, groves, and forests exist; the death, migration, and birth of sentient beings therein, and however many distinct destinations of rebirth exist; however many of their breaths circulate inward and outward; and however many times they open and close their eyes; all these and all other such things, the Tathāgata <note>an epithet of the Buddha, meaning One Who Has Thus Gone</note> knows through direct perception, discerning them as if counting them in a single moment.

Regarding what is called <term>dhāraṇī</term>: as previously mentioned in the description of the qualities of a Bodhisattva, there are four types: the dhāraṇī of patience, the dhāraṇī of dharma <gloss>teachings</gloss>, the dhāraṇī of meaning, and the dhāraṇī of mantra. When it is said, "O sons of the gods, it is because all phenomena are utterly pure," the term "purity" here refers to the very absence of any entity <note>original: "bhāva"</note>. It is a synonym for saying they are "utterly non-existent."

As for the statement, "Blessed One, it is not difficult to attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment," this is because all phenomena are non-existent. It is not difficult to realize that a non-entity is indeed a non-entity. However, it is difficult to realize the true nature of phenomena if they were held to exist. If phenomena were existent, one would have to practice the Perfections <note>original: "pāramitā"</note> and other conducts in order to increase virtuous qualities and abandon non-virtuous qualities. But since these phenomena do not exist, the practice is not difficult. Therefore, it is said that attaining enlightenment is not difficult.

The intention behind the Elder Shariputra’s statement that attaining enlightenment is difficult is as follows: If it were enough to simply remain in silence after realizing that all phenomena are by nature non-existent entities, like space, then it would not be difficult. Why was this <term>sutra</term> <gloss>scripture</gloss> composed, which states: A <term>bodhisattva mahasattva</term> <gloss>great awakening being</gloss> should not abandon these four qualities for as long as they live, even for the sake of their own life? 

It was composed to correctly show the method for attaining unsurpassed awakening to those who are confused about how to properly enter the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss>. It is to cause those who are heedless to correctly take it up, to truly encourage those who are discouraged, and to bring genuine joy to those who have correctly entered.

The number four is mentioned specifically to prevent people from refusing to listen out of fear that the subject is too vast. Mentioning the number also allows for easy memorization. Furthermore, patience and gentleness, which appear below, share the same purpose and are thus not differentiated as separate categories.

Although there are many ways to categorize those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle, two names <note>bodhisattva and mahasattva</note> are mentioned for three reasons: through aspiration, through application, and through understanding.

How is it through aspiration? They are a <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>awakening being</gloss> because they aspire toward the profound objects of knowledge. They are a <term>mahasattva</term> <gloss>great being</gloss> because they aspire toward great power.

How is it through application? It is because they exert themselves for the sake of their own unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and to completely protect all sentient beings from suffering.

How is it through understanding? It is because awakening is realized through two strengths. What are these two? They are the strength of intelligence and the strength of diligence. One cannot realize awakening with ignorance or with little diligence.

### ON ALCHEMY.

<margin>The goal of Alchemy is not gold and silver, but secrets.</margin>

I do not write so extensively about Alchemy in vain, but I do so with this intent and end: that from these things you may nearly and solidly learn what lies hidden within it, and how it ought to be understood. Nor should you be offended that neither gold nor silver comes forth from it. Rather, care must be taken that through it <term>arcana</term> <gloss>hidden secrets/healing powers</gloss> are uncovered, and the deceptions of the <term>seplasiarii</term> <gloss>perfumers or ointment-sellers</gloss> are exposed, by which the unrefined common people are deceived, while these men supply for one florin what they would not redeem for a single penny. So precious are their secrets.

<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and inherent even in the best things? All are compelled to confess this. Therefore, if this is true, I now ask of you: must not the poison be separated from the good and the useful? And the good be taken, the evil left behind? Truly indeed, it must be so. If it is necessary, then I ask you to explain to me how that separation is performed in your workshops? For among you, all things remain mixed together. But to protect your simplicity—if you are forced to confess that poison lurks there and are asked where it eventually goes—then you bring forth some nonsense about "corrections" which supposedly drive out and take away the poison, <margin>The correction of the Physicians is discussed.</margin> just as they say Quince corrects Scammony <note>a harsh purgative resin</note>, or as <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>a preparation of scammony juice</gloss> is said to do. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you meanwhile boast that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. But where has it gone? <margin>Diagridion.</margin> It remains in the <term>Diagridion</term>. Try it, if you are wise: exceed the limit, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know it quickly enough. Thus you also "correct" <term>Turbith</term> <gloss>an East Indian root used as a purgative</gloss> and call it <term>Diaturbith</term>. Such are your corrections, which would be fit for peasants and should be given to pack-horses. Make the danger by exceeding the limit and increase the dose: you will see whether you do not feel the poison. <margin>What it is to correct as a Physician.</margin> *To correct is to take what has been corrected.* If a man is malicious and has sinned, and if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of him who was punished lasts. Such are these corrections; the status remains with the substances, not with you. Now indeed, in this case, a Physician must consider nothing further than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation. As, for example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted for food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it without harm. The same must be understood equally of all other things, namely that there is a need for a similar separation. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation—unless by chance nature happens to supply your deficiencies, or a greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection remains.

Now then, finally, that true foundation is necessary which removes the poison, just as Alchemy provides. For it must be done in such a way that, if Mars is in the Sun, Mars is removed; and if Saturn is in Venus, it is separated from her <note>referring to removing metallic impurities or balancing astrological/chemical influences</note>. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies exist in them. But when bodies are contrary, it is entirely necessary that some of them be removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety is abolished, and the evil you seek to avoid is taken from the good. <margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin> As gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so Medicine is much less useful if it does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary that all things pass through fire into a second generation, by which it ought to benefit and help man. And should this not rightly be judged the upright foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought to apply not poisons, but secrets. <margin>The workshops are rebuked.</margin> Moreover, all those workshop preparations, however many of them there are, do not contribute even a tiny letter to this doctrine. Instead, they are simply occupied in "correcting," as if a dog farts in a room and that stench is quelled either by lozenges and incense or by juniper wood—I ask you, does not the stench remain in the room afterward just as much as before? And although it may not be perceived by smell, is it therefore lawful for anyone to say the stench has been separated and no longer remains? On the contrary, it is present, but "corrected" by the fumigation. Thus the fumigation and the foul air enter the nostrils together. Such also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who blunt an <term>aleopaticum</term> <note>a bitter or purging medicine</note> with sugar so that it inflicts no harm. Thus sugar and honey are their entire <term>magistery</term> <gloss>mastery/chemical achievement</gloss>. Thus they also "correct" gentian with treacle. Are these not the works of asinine ignorance?
